title: The Best Case Fallacy
author: Didau, David
summary: David Didau applies philosopher Roger Scruton's critique of "unscrupulous optimism" to education leadership and policy, arguing that what Scruton calls the "best case fallacy" — the habit of imagining the most favorable outcome and treating it as a plan — routinely drives catastrophic school decisions. Using the $1.3 billion LAUSD iPad rollout and a string of similar technology failures as case studies, Didau demonstrates that unscrupulous optimism isn't a rare error but an endemic feature of school reform: new policies launch without pilots, evaluation plans, or honest reckonings with systemic constraints. He draws on Rob Coe's 2013 finding that most claimed school improvement is illusory and most widely-advocated improvement strategies are not robustly proven, a verdict he argues flows directly from leaders refusing to acknowledge the worst case alongside the best. Didau's counter-position is not pessimism but "judicious pessimism" in Scruton's sense: maintaining the structures and procedures through which mistakes are identified and corrected, rather than optimistically redesigning systems under the belief that the new arrangement will be free of error. The article closes with the coursework debate as a live example of the fallacy at work: the seductive principle collides with the predictable incentive effects that make the system less fair and less reliable the moment coursework is high-stakes.
points: The "best case fallacy" is not a personal cognitive failure but a systemic property: when education leaders habitually estimate the best outcome and plan for it, ordinary well-intentioned actors responding to incentives produce predictable disasters — as the LAUSD iPad debacle and successive device-rollout failures demonstrate.

Rob Coe's 2013 evidence-base finding is the most uncomfortable implication of Didau's argument: most claimed school improvement is illusory, and most widely-advocated improvement strategies are not robustly proven — meaning optimism-driven reform has historically been gambling with children's futures rather than investing in them.

Didau's analysis of the coursework debate shows how the best case fallacy survives contact with evidence: the principle (authenticity, range of skills) is sound, but once coursework is high-stakes every incentive shifts — parents help, tutors rewrite, AI drafts — and the grade stops reflecting attainment.

Teacher assessment reform is doubly risky because research consistently finds teacher judgements can disadvantage students from poorer backgrounds and some ethnic minority groups relative to external exams — meaning more teacher judgement is not a neutral equity move.

The antidote is not pessimism but judicious pessimism: keeping open the institutions, customs, and procedures through which mistakes are corrected and faults confessed, rather than replacing them with new arrangements optimistically imagined to be error-free.
quotes: If we always look on the bright side of life then we fall into 'the best case fallacy'. In Scruton's words, this leads inexorably to "a kind of addiction to unreality that informs the most destructive forms of optimism: a desire to cross out reality, as the premise from which practical reason begins, and to replace it with a system of compliant illusions.
Unscrupulous optimism doesn't just distort our private decisions; it shapes public policy, institutional reform and billion dollar procurement programmes.
We routinely launch new policies, spend money on new systems, train teachers in trendy-sounding pedagogical gimmickry and almost never run pilot programmes, or have a clear evaluation plan in place.

Without such an honest and critical appraisal of our efforts we're gambling with children's futures. And the problem with gamblers is that they don't actually see themselves as risk-takers. They convince themselves that they can beat the odds, that they've discovered a fool-proof system to buck the odds.

Judicious pessimism teaches us not to idolise human beings, but to forgive them their faults and to strive in private for their amendments. It teaches us to limit our ambitions in the public sphere, and to keep open the institutions, customs and procedures whereby mistakes are corrected and faults confessed to, rather than aim for some new arrangement in which mistakes are never made.

Complex systems don't fail because individuals behave badly but because ordinary people respond predictably to the incentives the system creates. To hope that everyone will exercise restraint is a wager against human nature, and history suggests it's a very poor bet.
